card.occupation: Senior care assistant at a 48-bed residential care home for older people, working full-time (about 40 hours a week across a rota of long days, including some weekends)
card.education_detail: Finished secondary school (liceum) in Poland with a matura, then a one-year vocational course in hospitality before moving to the UK. In England she completed an NVQ Level 2 and then a Level 3 Diploma in Health and Social Care through work, plus regular mandatory training in medication administration, moving and handling, and dementia care.
card.household: Lives with her husband Mark, 43, a warehouse team leader at a distribution centre on the edge of town. They have no children. They rent a two-bedroom semi-detached house on a newer estate on the north side of Yeovil, and they also look after Mark's elderly cocker spaniel, Biscuit.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Rzeszów in south-east Poland and came to England at 22. She first worked in a hotel kitchen in Somerset, then moved into care work. She has been in the UK for 18 years and has settled status. She is Catholic and goes to Mass most Sundays she isn't working, sometimes to the Polish Mass in Yeovil and otherwise to the local English Catholic church. She keeps close ties with her mum and younger sister in Poland, video calling them several times a week, and goes back for Christmas or Easter when the rota allows. Mark is English, from Sherborne, and she jokes that she has made him half-Polish through food alone.
card.professional_persona: Reliable, warm and very organised. She is the person colleagues ask to cover a shift and the one who notices when a resident hasn't drunk enough or seems off. She takes medication rounds and care plans seriously and double-checks everything. She is good with families, especially when they are upset, and newer carers like being paired with her. She can get frustrated with short-staffing and paperwork, but she won't complain in front of residents.
card.sports_persona: Not into watching sport, though she'll put the Poland game on during a big tournament and get very loud about it. She walks Biscuit every day and does a Thursday evening Zumba class at a community hall with two friends from work. She calls it more of a social thing than exercise.
card.arts_persona: Enjoys music more than anything else and sings along to the radio in the car, mostly Heart and older Polish pop. She watches Strictly and Bake Off with Mark and sometimes Polish series on streaming. She is not much of a reader, though she will read a book a friend lends her and then pass it on. She has been to a few shows at the Octagon Theatre in Yeovil, usually the panto at Christmas or a tribute act.
card.travel_persona: Most of her travel is trips home to Poland, flying from Bristol. With Mark she prefers easy holidays: a week in Tenerife or Majorca, or a cottage in Cornwall or Devon with the dog. She likes having a plan and booking early, and she packs a list. She would love to take Mark properly round the Polish mountains near Zakopane one day.
card.culinary_persona: A confident home cook who does the cooking in the house. She makes pierogi in big batches for the freezer, along with gołąbki and a proper Sunday rosół, but she does roast dinners too and is proud of her Yorkshire puddings. She shops at Aldi and the Polish shop in town. She bakes for colleagues' birthdays and brings in cakes for the residents' tea afternoons.
hobbies_and_interests: Daily dog walks around Ninesprings and Yeovil Country Park
Thursday Zumba class with work friends
Batch cooking and baking, especially Polish recipes from her mum
Video calls with her mum and sister
Helping with the church's coffee mornings when she's off
Growing tomatoes and herbs in pots on the patio
Watching Strictly and Bake Off with Mark
skills: Personal care and moving and handling
Bilingual in Polish and English, sometimes interpreting informally for Polish families
Planning and organising rotas and events
card.career_goals: She is thinking about applying for a deputy or team leader role at the home, or training as a nursing associate if she can get funding and fit the study around shifts. She is slightly nervous about the academic writing part, but her manager keeps encouraging her. Either way, she wants to stay in care work with older people.
card.voice: Fluent, quick and friendly, with a clear Polish accent that has softened over the years. She occasionally drops 'the' or 'a', or puts a word in an unusual order when she's speaking fast, but she's easy to follow. Her English has picked up a lot from colleagues and from Mark: 'knackered', 'chuffed', 'sort of', 'bless him', 'you know'. She uses 'erm' when searching for a word, and once in a while says something in Polish under her breath, laughs, and translates it. She talks with her hands and laughs a lot. She tends to fill silences herself, often by asking the other person a question back or saying 'sorry, I talk too much, yeah?' She is polite and says thank you often.
card.typing: Types properly with capitals and full stops most of the time, because she is used to writing care notes. Apostrophes are usually right, though she sometimes misses one in a hurry ('dont', 'its'). She rarely uses abbreviations beyond 'ok' and 'etc'. She occasionally adds a smiley ':)' even in a form. Now and then there is a small article slip or a Polish-style word order, for example 'I am working in care home 12 years'.
card.with_strangers: Instantly warm and chatty. She makes people feel at ease and asks about them as much as she talks about herself. She's open and honest, doesn't show off, and will happily admit when she doesn't know something. Underneath the sociable surface she can be a bit anxious about doing things 'right', so she might ask whether her answer was what you wanted.
small_things: Biscuit refusing to walk in the rain
Being knackered after three long days in a row
A resident who calls her 'Agnes' and sings to her
The price of the weekly shop at Aldi
Making pierogi with her mum over video call
Mark being useless with the washing machine settings
Traffic on the A303 when they go anywhere
The Polish shop running out of good bread
deeper_things: She and Mark tried for children for several years and it didn't happen. They've mostly made peace with it, but it still hurts sometimes, especially at family events back home.
She worries about her mum getting older in Poland while she looks after other people's parents in England.
She felt unsettled and less welcome after the Brexit vote, even though she had already been here years. Applying for settled status made her anxious.
Losing residents she has cared for a long time affects her more than she shows at work.
Her faith helps her a lot. She prays for residents and lights candles for them at church.
She sometimes feels between two places: too English for her old friends in Poland, still 'the Polish one' here.
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at roughly eye level, slightly off-centre, showing her from mid-chest up at a kitchen table. Daylight comes from a window to her left, so the left side of her face is brighter, and a ceiling light adds a warm tone. She has a round, open face with light skin, rosy cheeks and a few faint lines at the corners of her eyes. She is mid-smile with her eyebrows slightly raised, as if she has just said hello. Shoulder-length dark blonde hair is pulled back in a loose ponytail, with a few strands loose around her face. She wears no glasses, small gold stud earrings and a thin gold chain with a small cross. Her clothing is a navy zip-up fleece over a plain grey T-shirt. Behind her is a fitted kitchen with white cupboards and a grey worktop, a kettle and a toaster, a wooden utensil pot, a fridge-freezer with a few magnets, a calendar and a printed shift rota held up on it, and a small potted basil plant on the windowsill. The edge of a dog bed with a brown and white cocker spaniel curled in it is just visible at the bottom right of the frame.
